processing: Pu-erh, raw or ripe, sifted, steamed and pressed into 357 g cakes, wrapped in paper and stacked seven to a bamboo-leaf tong.
harvest_season: Depends on the tea pressed; spring and autumn pickings are the most valued for pu-erh.
appearance_dry: Round discs about 20 cm wide, domed with a dimple underneath, olive to brown when raw and glossy red-brown when ripe.
appearance_liquor: Raw is bright red-gold when it has some age; ripe is deep, clear red.
appearance_wet: Thick large-leaf pieces, brown-green in raw tea and dark brown in ripe.
taste_profile: Raw pressings are full, clean and smooth with a sweet return and a bright finish; ripe ones are thick and sweet with an aged, longan-like note.

brewing.notes: Flake gently off the edge and rinse once. For ripe pressings use boiling water; for very young raw, shorten the steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year, as single cakes or as a seven-cake tong, and meant for keeping. Sellers often price raw and ripe by age, with five to ten years of storage common and twenty-year cakes scarce. The words on the wrapper are a format and an old trade name, not a mark of grade or age, and they are printed on all sorts of tea.
description:
Qizi Bing Cha, seven-sons cake tea, is the standard pu-erh format: a cake of about 357 grams, seven to a stack, which adds up to 2.5 kilograms. It describes the packing, so both raw and ripe tea can wear the name.

The cakes are pressed from sifted pu-erh and wrapped in paper, then seven are bound in bamboo leaf into a tong. Those tongs are what the old trade moved, and they still suit long storage.

How it drinks depends on what is inside. Raw pressings start bright and bitter-sweet and soften over time, while ripe ones are thick and sweet from the start. Treat one as you would any cake: flake, rinse, and keep the first steeps quick.

Don't take the phrase on a wrapper as a guarantee. Look for the factory, region and year, and be careful with 'old' cakes, whose paper can be faked. A whole tong makes sense only once you have tried a single cake.

The seven is also a story. In Yunnan the number is read as lucky, and cakes are given at weddings and festivals as a wish for many children and a united family.
history:
The name began as a unit of measure. In the Yongzheng reign of the Qing, Yunnan's tea traders sold seven round cakes to a tong, a standard set by the government to regulate production and transport. The late Qing brought other formats, and in the early Republic local tea guilds tried to bring weights back in line.

After 1949, state factories under the China Tea company pressed 'Zhongcha' yuan cha, round tea. In 1970 the Yunnan tea import and export company swapped 'round' for 'cake', adopted the lucky seven for gift appeal, and registered Qizi Bing Cha to replace the older brand. Later accounts tying the tea to the Zhou dynasty or to the Qianlong Emperor's praise are best read as sales lore.
